title: Singular Countable Nouns, A/An and Some
summary: Use a/an and other determiners with singular countable nouns, but use bare plurals for general categories. Describe jobs and characteristics, and distinguish some meaning an unspecified number from some meaning not all.
learningObjectives: Use a/an or another determiner with singular countable nouns and choose the correct plural form.
Name professions and describe individual characteristics using a/an where needed.
Make general statements with plural nouns without inserting some unnecessarily.
Use some with plurals to describe particular items or a subset rather than a whole category.

explanation.heading: Singular countable nouns require a determiner
explanation.body: Countable nouns name people or items that can normally be counted. A singular countable noun usually needs a determiner such as a, an, the, this or my in a complete noun phrase. Use a before a consonant sound and an before a vowel sound; the sound, not the first written letter, determines the choice. Plural countable nouns can appear with a number, a determiner or no article.
explanation.example: I borrowed an atlas, and my classmates borrowed two maps.

explanation.heading: Use a/an to identify a kind of person or thing
explanation.body: Use a/an with a singular countable noun when identifying its type, role or classification. Jobs usually follow this pattern after be, become or work as: a designer, an editor. With plural subjects, use plural job nouns without a/an: they are designers. Classification statements can also use bare plurals to refer to a group generally.
explanation.example: Priya is an illustrator, but her brothers are photographers.

explanation.heading: Descriptions: a single feature versus plural features
explanation.body: When a feature is a single countable part, a/an can be needed: a friendly smile, an unusual voice or a long neck. Plural features do not take a/an: bright eyes or strong hands. Do not automatically add an article simply because an adjective comes before a plural noun.
explanation.example: The actor has a warm smile and expressive eyes.

explanation.heading: Bare plurals refer to categories in general
explanation.body: Use a bare plural noun when making a broad statement about members of a category. For example, bicycles can be useful transport or librarians help people find books. In these contexts, some would normally introduce a limited group rather than describe the category as a whole. Bare plurals also follow plural forms of be when identifying occupations.

explanation.heading: Some can mean a number or not all
explanation.body: Use some with plural countable nouns for an unspecified number of particular people or things: I met some visitors after the talk. In many ordinary contexts some is optional, but it signals that the speaker is referring to a particular collection. Some also contrasts a subset with the rest of a group: some applicants have experience, while others are new. Do not confuse this limited meaning with a general statement about everyone in a category.
explanation.example: Some volunteers arrived early, but the others came after lunch.

comparisons.title: One member of a type versus a plural category

left.label: Singular identification
left.note: A names one person's profession and precedes a singular countable noun.

right.label: Plural identification
right.note: A/an is not used before the plural profession biologists.

comparisons.title: Talking about a whole category versus a subset

left.label: General category
left.note: The bare plural makes a statement about koalas as a category.

right.label: Limited group
right.example: Some koalas live near protected forests.
right.note: Some refers to a subset, not necessarily every koala.

examples.sentence: My cousin is a paramedic at the local hospital.
examples.note: Paramedic is a singular profession, so it takes a.

examples.sentence: Hugo has an unusual accent and a friendly voice.
examples.note: Both accent and voice are singular countable nouns; their articles follow sound.

examples.sentence: Owls are birds that usually hunt at night.
examples.note: Owls appears without some because the sentence classifies a whole type of animal.

examples.sentence: I ordered some notebooks for the new trainees.
examples.note: Some identifies an unspecified number of particular notebooks.

examples.sentence: Some members joined online, while others attended in person.
examples.note: Some contrasts part of a group with the rest.

commonMistakes.why: A singular profession requires an article; engineer begins with a vowel sound.
Do not use a before a plural profession.
The plural countable noun paintings cannot be introduced by a; the plural exclamation needs no article.

commonMistakes.incorrect: We need some new umbrella for the trip.
commonMistakes.correct: We need a new umbrella for the trip.
commonMistakes.why: Umbrella is singular, so some with a plural-countable meaning cannot modify it; a agrees with the following word new.

studyTips: For each singular count noun, check whether a determiner is present. Choose a/an by the sound at the start of the next word.
Practise changing one-person job descriptions to plural descriptions: an engineer → engineers; a nurse → nurses.
Compare two statements aloud: Bees are insects (a general classification); some bees live alone (a particular subset).

exercises.prompt: Tariq works as ___ architect in a design studio.
exercises.feedback: Architect is a singular occupation beginning with a vowel sound, so use an.

exercises.prompt: The two sisters work in healthcare. They are ___.
exercises.feedback: A plural subject describing a profession needs a plural count noun without a/an.

exercises.prompt: Complete this general classification about the whole category: ___ are mammals.
exercises.feedback: The bare plural Dolphins presents a general classification; some would restrict the claim to a subset.

exercises.prompt: I met ___ designers from Lisbon at a conference yesterday.
exercises.feedback: Some describes an unspecified number of particular designers; designers is plural.

exercises.prompt: Amira is ___ (accountant). Write the article and singular job noun.
exercises.feedback: An accountant is the natural singular job description; accountant begins with a vowel sound.

exercises.prompt: The exhibition includes ___ (painting). Write some followed by the plural noun.
exercises.feedback: Some paintings refers to an unspecified number of countable artworks.

exercises.prompt: The singer has ___ (short beard). Write the article, adjective and noun.
exercises.feedback: Beard is a single countable feature, and short begins with a consonant sound.

exercises.prompt: ___ (elephant) are large mammals. Write the bare plural noun for a general classification.
exercises.feedback: A bare plural can name a category in general without some.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence by adding the missing article: Nora is doctor at the community clinic.
acceptedAnswers: Nora is a doctor at the community clinic.
exercises.feedback: The singular profession doctor needs a in this description.

exercises.prompt: Correct only the article: What a beautiful paintings!
exercises.feedback: The plural noun paintings cannot take a; remove the article.

exercises.prompt: Correct only the determiner: He bought some new umbrella yesterday.
acceptedAnswers: He bought a new umbrella yesterday.
exercises.feedback: New umbrella is one singular countable item; use a before new.

exercises.prompt: Correct only the article: My friends are a talented musicians.
exercises.feedback: Musicians is plural, so do not put a before the adjective and noun.

speakingExercises.prompt: State Lena’s job in one complete sentence. Use the exact facts “Lena / be / pilot” and begin “Lena is”.
speakingExercises.feedback: A pilot identifies a singular profession.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say one sentence with these facts: Zara / be / an engineer. Begin “Zara is”.
speakingExercises.feedback: Engineer takes an because its first sound is a vowel.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct the article and say the full sentence, changing nothing else: “Mia is a accountant.”
speakingExercises.feedback: The profession accountant begins with a vowel sound, so an replaces a.

speakingExercises.prompt: Two neighbours have the same job. State the facts in one sentence: both neighbours / architects. Begin “They are”.
speakingExercises.feedback: The plural job name architects has no a/an.

speakingExercises.prompt: Report a past meeting in one sentence: I / spoke to / some exchange students / yesterday. Keep the given wording.
acceptedAnswers: I spoke to some exchange students yesterday.
speakingExercises.feedback: Some refers to a particular, unspecified number of students.

speakingExercises.prompt: Give a general classification using the exact facts: sparrows / are / birds. Begin “Sparrows”.
speakingExercises.feedback: The bare plural refers to the category as a whole.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say exactly two sentences with these facts. First: “Students in this group study English.” Second: some students / also speak / French. Keep this order and begin the second sentence “Some students”.
acceptedAnswers: Students in this group study English. Some students also speak French.
speakingExercises.feedback: The first statement applies to the whole group; the second identifies a subset.

speakingExercises.prompt: Describe Dina in one complete sentence. Begin “Dina has” and use the exact features “a round face” and “green eyes”, joined with “and”.
acceptedAnswers: Dina has a round face and green eyes.
speakingExercises.feedback: Use a for the single countable feature face, but no article before plural eyes.

listeningExercises.audioText: Asha is an engineer, and her two brothers are musicians.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which statement correctly identifies their jobs?
choices: Asha is a musician and her brothers are engineers.
Asha is an engineer and her brothers are musicians.
listeningExercises.feedback: An engineer identifies Asha’s job; musicians identifies the brothers’ jobs.

listeningExercises.audioText: I packed some extra notebooks for the workshop, but I forgot the coloured markers.
listeningExercises.feedback: The speaker packed notebooks but specifically forgot the markers.

listeningExercises.audioText: My uncle is an optician at a small shop.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word occupation phrase immediately after “is”.
listeningExercises.feedback: An optician is the audible phrase identifying the uncle’s profession.

listeningExercises.audioText: All members joined the induction meeting, but some members stayed afterwards to ask questions.
listeningExercises.feedback: Some members refers to a subset of those who attended, not everyone.

listeningExercises.audioText: Owen has a narrow face and dark eyes, while his brother has a broad face and brown eyes.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which feature describes Owen, not his brother?
listeningExercises.feedback: A narrow face is Owen’s feature; broad face and brown eyes describe his brother.

listeningExercises.audioText: Three visitors are researchers, and their guide is a historian.
listeningExercises.feedback: The audio identifies the guide as a historian, distinct from the visitors who are researchers.

listeningExercises.audioText: We need some spare batteries for the remote controls.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three-word noun phrase immediately after “need”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Some spare batteries refers to an unspecified number of particular batteries.

listeningExercises.audioText: I saw some dolphins near the harbour entrance.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word noun phrase immediately after “saw”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Some dolphins indicates a number of animals observed in that particular situation.
